habit_line: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Good morning, inquirers! Today everything turns: you, the hands of a clock, and a robot. An angle tells us how much something has turned.
Remember: notice it, test it with a protractor or a paper clock, explain why.
do: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Everybody stand up and face the front. The front is North. Ready? Quarter turn clockwise! Which way are you facing now?
Back to North. Half turn! Now 45 degrees anticlockwise: just half of a quarter turn. Where are you facing?
On a clock, which o’clock times do you think make a right angle between the hands? Write down your guess before you try.
stuck: Stuck: put the minute hand on 12. Move only the hour hand, one number at a time.
Not sure if it is a right angle: hold the corner of a square of paper between the hands.
Finished early: what is the angle at 1 o’clock? How can you work it out without a protractor?

say: “I estimate first. This angle is a bit smaller than a right angle, so about 60 or 70 degrees. I put the centre of the protractor on the vertex and the baseline along one arm. That arm points to 0 on the inside scale, so I count up the inside scale: 10, 20 … 65. Not 115: my estimate says it is smaller than 90.”

“A clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees, cut into 12 equal spaces. 360 divided by 12 is 30. At 2 o’clock the hands are 2 spaces apart: 60 degrees. At 10 o’clock I go the shorter way: also 2 spaces, 60 degrees.”
“I face North-West. I turn 135 degrees clockwise. Each step on the compass is 45 degrees, so 135 is 3 steps: North, North-East, East. I face East.”

do: Ask: “Is this angle bigger or smaller than a right angle? So which number on the protractor makes sense?”
Ask: “How many spaces apart are the hands? How many degrees is one space?”
Ask: “How many 45° steps is that turn? Which way: clockwise or anticlockwise?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Estimate first: compare with the corner of a page (90°).”
Hint 2: “Draw the clock or the compass and count the spaces or steps with your pencil.”
Hint 3: “For a corner of a square or rectangle: the parts add up to 90°. Take away the parts you know.”

say: “Is turning 270° clockwise the same as turning 90° anticlockwise? Test it: stand up and do both.”
ask: “Is turning 270° clockwise the same as turning 90° anticlockwise? Test it: stand up and do both.”
Yes: 270° clockwise and 90° anticlockwise make a full turn (360°) together, so you end up facing the same way.

say: “Today you estimated before you measured, counted spaces on a clock and steps on a compass, and found every angle in a fan. Inquirers check with an estimate. Well done!”

p4l6-title.note: Objective: Estimate and measure angles with a protractor, find every angle in a fan of rays, work out angles between clock hands (30° for each space) and turns of the minute hand (6° a minute), turn on the 8-point compass (45° steps) and work backwards from a turn, and find unknown angles in squares and rectangles. Thinking strategies today: ESTIMATE FIRST (compare with 90° and 180°), COUNT THE TURN (12 clock spaces, 8 compass steps), WORK IN ORDER (every angle in a fan), WORK BACKWARDS (undo a turn). Materials: A clear 180° protractor and a 30 cm ruler for each child (a plastic school protractor is fine, cheap to buy; families bring one from home; keep two or three spares), a paper clock with a split pin (or a real clock), a square of paper for checking right angles, mini whiteboards, a compass card on the floor or wall. Online: children use their own protractor and a paper clock at home; the screen is North for the turning games, and children stand and turn on camera. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 3-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 23 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 23 to 30.5 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 30.5 to 34 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 34 to 80: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) (the first 2 minutes are the protractor demo) 34 to 51.5, check together 51.5 to 53, short teaching before page 2 53 to 55.5, page 2 on your own 55.5 to 77.5 (the last 3 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 77.5 to 80. Talk time 80 to 84.5 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 84.5 to 87.5. Looking back 87.5 to 90 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). This page ends at question 2. After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today's tool is Draw it. Draw a picture, bar model or number line that shows what is known and what is asked. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p4l6-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 2 quarter turns, which is a half turn. You are facing the opposite way (your back is to the screen). 2) 55°. A square corner is 90°, and 90° − 35° = 55°. A GOOD REASON: A square corner is 90° and a half turn is 180°. Angles side by side add up to the whole turn. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "This page ends at question 2. After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l6-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Robot turns. Everyone stands and faces the front of the room: that is North (online: the screen is North). Read each call; children turn, then point and say the direction they face. Click to show it. Start every call from North. If time allows play a faster round without the slide: "From where you are now: quarter turn anticlockwise! Half turn! 45° clockwise!" Children who end up facing the wrong way watch a partner and try again. Listen for children who say "clockwise is the way the clock hands go". Online: on a mirrored self-view a turn looks reversed, so say "turn to your right" for clockwise, and tell children to ignore their own picture.

p4l6-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Three questions, about 30 seconds each: write it, say the answer together on three, then click. No follow-up questions. 1) 90°. 2) 180°: two right angles. 3) 4, so a full turn is 4 × 90° = 360°. The other two warm-up questions (face N, quarter turn anticlockwise; a 3/4 turn or 250°) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l6-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 20.5. Pairs use a paper clock (online: a paper clock at home or a real clock). Ask them to predict first: which times make a right angle? Most children say 3 o’clock; fewer think of 9 o’clock. They check each time with the corner of a square of paper. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: what is the angle at 1 o’clock? At 2 o’clock? Can you work it out without a protractor? GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if the clock shows half past three (3:30)? Is the angle still 90°? Why not? Answer: No. It is 75°: at 3:30 the hour hand has moved halfway from 3 to 4, which is 15° past the 3. The minute hand points at 6 (180°) and the hour hand at 105°.

p4l6-explore2.note: Minutes 20.5 to 23. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather the pairs. Two debrief questions only. Answers: 1) 3 o’clock and 9 o’clock (3 spaces apart either way). 2) 6 o’clock: a straight line, a half turn, 180°. The third question (the angle at 1 o’clock, 30°: a full turn is 360° and the clock face has 12 equal spaces, so 360 ÷ 12 = 30; check: 3 o’clock is 3 spaces, 3 × 30 = 90) is not asked; the first teaching slide after the break uses it. Many children say 12 o’clock is a straight line too: the hands are on top of each other, so the angle is 0°. Keep the 30° idea: we use it after the break.

p4l6-teach1.note: Teach. Hold up a real protractor. Ask first: "Is this angle bigger or smaller than a right angle?" (smaller: estimate about 60°). Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "The bottom arm points to 0 on the INSIDE scale, so I count up the inside scale: 10, 20 … 60, 65. The outside scale says 115 at the same place, but 115 is more than a right angle and my estimate says less. So the angle is 65°." Online: children measure the angle on their screen with a real protractor if the screen is large enough, or on the worksheet later. Point out: the length of the arms does not change the angle.

p4l6-teach2.note: Teach. Children stand facing the front (North) and act it out. Think-aloud: "I face North-West. Each step on the compass is 45 degrees, so 135 degrees is 3 steps. Clockwise is the way clock hands go: North, North-East, East. I face East." Common mistake: counting NW itself as the first step. Point with a finger: move first, then count. Then the second example: 225° is 5 steps; anticlockwise from E: NE, N, NW, W, SW. Getting back from SW to E is 225° clockwise, or 135° anticlockwise, the shorter way.

p4l6-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 1 step: NE. b) A 3/4 turn is 270° = 6 steps clockwise from S: SW, W, NW, N, NE, E. Or think: 3/4 clockwise is the same as 1/4 anticlockwise, and 1/4 anticlockwise from S is E. c) Clockwise from E to NW is 5 steps (225°); anticlockwise is 3 steps (135°), so the smallest turn is 135° anticlockwise.

p4l6-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Reading the wrong protractor scale (40° written as 140°) instead of starting from the 0 on the arm and checking with an estimate. (2) Counting the numbers on the clock instead of the spaces between them, or measuring the bigger way round (210° instead of 150° at 7 o’clock). (3) Compass turns: mixing up clockwise and anticlockwise, or counting the starting direction as the first 45° step.

p4l6-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 34): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Online: children stand in view of the camera; the screen is North. Finish with "Turn to face the screen" from different directions: who turned the smallest way?

p4l6-teachfan.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q2 has 4 rays). Online: many cameras show a mirrored self-view, so left and right can look swapped when a child shows a protractor or points an arm; check against the shared slide, not the video tile. Name angles with three letters: the middle letter is always the vertex O. Think-aloud: "First the small angles that sit next to each other: 20° and 50°. Then two together: 20 + 50 = 70°. With 3 rays there are 3 angles." Do NOT give the number of angles for 4 rays: let pairs find it on the worksheet. Hint for strugglers: "Start from OA. List every angle that starts at OA, then every angle that starts at OB …"

p4l6-ws1.note: Minutes 36 to 51.5. Pair task for Q1: each child estimates and measures two of the four angles, then checks the partner's two (about 4.5 minutes, not 8). Walk around and watch protractors: centre on the vertex, baseline on an arm, count from 0. Ask "Does your answer match your estimate?" Q1c and d are turned, so children must turn the protractor (or the page). Accept answers within 2°. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "This page ends at question 2. After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l6-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1: accept 2° either way. If a child wrote 140° for a, ask "Is a bigger than a right angle?" Q2: work in order. Small angles: ∠AOB 30°, ∠BOC 60°, ∠COD 45°. Two together: ∠AOC = 30 + 60 = 90°, ∠BOD = 60 + 45 = 105°. All three: ∠AOD = 30 + 60 + 45 = 135°. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 angles.

p4l6-teachclock.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3). Link back to explore: 3 o’clock was 90° = 3 spaces, so one space is 30°. Click 1: 2 o’clock. Click 2 shows 10 o’clock: "Is it 10 spaces? No: go the shorter way, from 10 to 12, 2 spaces." Then the minute hand: it goes all the way round (360°) in 60 minutes, so 360 ÷ 60 = 6° a minute, or 30° every 5 minutes. Count on with a paper clock: 6:05 to 6:20 is 3 jumps of 5 minutes, 3 × 30° = 90°.

p4l6-teachrect.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 has two parts; the third drawing, two squares, is an optional extension and is the idea behind Go further 9). Fold a square of paper to show the corner is a right angle. Click each answer after children try on whiteboards. Rectangle: the whole corner is 90°, so the missing part is 90 − 37 = 53°. Square cut in three: 90 − 20 − 45 = 25° (check 20 + 25 + 45 = 90). Two squares: the two right angles together make 180°, but the overlap of 40° is counted twice, so 180 − 40 = 140°. Act it out with two paper squares on top of each other.

p4l6-teachrobot.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4d works backwards; Q6a is the robot). Act it out: one child is the robot, the group reads the cards. To undo a turn, turn the same amount the other way, like taking off shoes after socks. Check Mei: start E, 90° clockwise is S ✓. For "find all pairs" (a Think harder question now): with three cards A, B, C the pairs are A and B, A and C, B and C. Example (not on the worksheet): cards 45° clockwise, 90° anticlockwise, 180°, from N to E. 45 + 180: SW, not this one. 45 cw and 90 acw: NW, not this one. 90 acw and 180: E ✓. Only one pair works.

p4l6-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially anyone who still counts the starting direction as a step or counts the numbers on the clock instead of the spaces. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q3 to Q6. Then choose a Think harder question. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 3 minutes of this block (minute 74.5 to 77.5) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l6-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3b: 7 o’clock is 5 spaces the shorter way (7 to 12), 150°, not 210°. The minute-hand question (3:10 to 3:35 is 25 minutes × 6° = 150°) is now a Think harder item, so the page has fewer parts. Q4b: 135° is 3 steps anticlockwise from SW: S, SE, E. Q4c: clockwise NE, E, SE, S is 3 steps (135°); anticlockwise would be 5 steps (225°). Q4d: undo 90° anticlockwise by turning 90° clockwise from NW: N, NE. Q5: 90 − 58 = 32; 90 − 15 − 48 = 27. (The overlapping-squares idea is now a Go further question.) Q6a: N → E → NE → SW. The "find ALL the pairs" question is now Think harder stretch 4: list all 6 pairs: 45+90 (SE), 45 cw + 135 acw (W ✓), 45+180 (SW), 90 cw + 135 acw (NW), 90+180 (W ✓), 135 acw + 180 (NE).

p4l6-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) N (225° is 5 steps of 45°: S, SW, W, NW, N) 2) 60° and 60°. Both are 2 spaces apart the shorter way. 3) 210° (35 minutes × 6°) 4) Two ways: 45° clockwise and 135° anticlockwise; or 90° clockwise and 180°.

p4l6-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 75°. At 3:30 the minute hand points to 6, but the hour hand is HALFWAY between 3 and 4 (half an hour has passed). From the hour hand to 4 is half a space (15°), from 4 to 6 is 2 spaces (60°): 75°. 2) 10 angles (4 small, 3 of two parts, 2 of three parts, 1 of four parts). Each small angle is 120 ÷ 4 = 30°, so the three-part angles are 90°: 2 right angles. More are in the question bank and on the Think harder pages.

p4l6-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: Q1, is the hour hand pointing exactly at 3? Why not? How far has it moved since 3 o’clock? Q2, how big is each small angle? How can you count the angles without missing one? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l6-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: many children say 90°, as if the hour hand still pointed at 3. Use a real clock: move the minute hand from 12 to 6 and watch the hour hand creep half way to 4. Q2: the list in order (by number of parts) is the same idea as the fan on page 1; 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 is a pattern worth noticing: with 6 rays it would be 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15.

p4l6-gap-fan.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM fan (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Triangles by size"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: List every way. SAY: Name the base points B, C, D, E. A triangle needs the top point and two base points. List the pairs in order. ASK: How do you know you have not missed one or counted one twice? LISTEN FOR: An ordered list BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE, or a count by size 1, 2, 3. Listen for a rule such as "choose 2 base points". Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 3 triangles of size 1, 2 of size 2, 1 of size 3. (b) 6 triangles altogether. WHY: Pairs of base points: BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE gives 6. By size: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): The top point is joined to 5 points on the base line. How many triangles? Answer: 10 (4 + 3 + 2 + 1).

p4l6-talk.note: Minutes 80 to 84.5. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then test it standing up: everyone faces North and does both turns. Answer: yes, you end up facing the same way (both from N end at W), because 270° + 90° = 360°, a full turn. The turns are different sizes, but the direction you end up facing is the same. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "Ben says the angle at 3 o’clock is smaller than at 9 o’clock because 3 is smaller than 9. Who agrees?" (both are 90°: 3 spaces the shorter way). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l6-exit.note: Minutes 84.5 to 87.5. Answers: SE (3 steps of 45°: NE, E, SE). 150° (5 spaces of 30°). Extension: find all the o’clock times when the smaller angle between the hands is more than 90° (4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 o’clock).

p4l6-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 87.5 to 90. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
